summary: On Resurrection Sunday evening, Jesus stands among His frightened disciples, shows His wounds, eats before them, and sends them as the Father sent Him.
key_insight: Jesus proved who He was by His wounds. He did not point to His face; He showed His hands, His feet and His side. The risen body still carries the marks of the cross, and by them His friends knew Him.
story: On the evening of that same day, the first day of the week, the disciples were gathered with the doors shut for fear of the Jews. {Jn} They were sitting at the table, {Mk} and the two from Emmaus were still telling what had happened on the road. {Lk}
Then Jesus Himself stood in the midst of them and said, “Peace to you.” But they were terrified and frightened, and supposed they had seen a spirit. {Lk}

He said to them, “Why are you troubled? And why do doubts arise in your hearts? Behold My hands and My feet, that it is I Myself. Handle Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have.” He showed them His hands and His feet {Lk} and His side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. {Jn}

While they still did not believe for joy, and marveled, He asked, “Have you any food here?” They gave Him a piece of a broiled fish and some honeycomb, and He took it and ate in their presence. {Lk} He also rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen Him after He had risen. {Mk}

Jesus said to them again, “Peace to you! As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.” Then He breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” {Jn}

But Thomas, called the Twin, one of the twelve, was not with them when Jesus came. When the others told him, “We have seen the Lord,” he answered, “Unless I see in His hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into His side, I will not believe.” {Jn}
differences: John alone mentions the shut doors, Jesus’ side, the sending, the breathing, the words about forgiving sins, and Thomas’s absence.
Luke alone records the fear that they were seeing a spirit, the invitation to handle Him, and Jesus eating fish in front of them.
Mark alone says Jesus rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart.
Luke says Jesus showed His hands and feet; John says His hands and His side.
Mark and Luke speak of “the eleven” (Mark 16:14; Luke 24:33); John says Thomas was not there.

fit.question: Mark says Jesus appeared to “the eleven,” and Luke says the eleven were gathered. But John says Thomas was absent, so only ten apostles were there. Which is right?

points.label: A name for the group
points.text: After Judas was gone, the apostles were known as “the eleven”; when Matthias was chosen, he “was numbered with the eleven apostles” (Acts 1:26). The phrase names the group, not a head count.

points.label: The same habit elsewhere
points.text: Paul says the risen Jesus was seen “by the twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:5), though Judas was dead, and John calls Thomas “one of the twelve” in this very passage (John 20:24). Group names held even when the number did not.

fit.note: A team keeps its name when one member is away. Each writer is accurate in his own way of speaking.
fit.short: “The eleven” was the apostles’ group name after Judas, not an exact head count. Paul even calls them “the twelve.”

fit.question: On this evening Jesus breathes on the disciples and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Yet Luke records Him telling them to wait in Jerusalem for “the Promise of My Father,” which came at Pentecost (Luke 24:49; Acts 2). When did they receive the Spirit?

points.label: A first gift, then the outpouring
points.text: Many hold that the disciples truly received the Spirit that evening for new life and for their mission, and that Pentecost brought the promised power and the public outpouring on the whole church.

points.label: An acted promise
points.text: Others see the breathing as a sign and pledge of what was coming, the way prophets acted out God’s word. They point to John’s note that the Spirit would be given when Jesus was glorified (John 7:39), and Jesus’ word that He must go away before the Helper would come (John 16:7).

fit.note: Faithful readers explain the two moments differently, but both accounts agree that the church’s mission depends on the Spirit whom Jesus gives.
fit.short: Some see a real first gift of the Spirit that evening, with power poured out at Pentecost; others see an acted promise of Pentecost.

scene.label: A ghost?
scene.text: Many people in Jesus’ day believed the dead could appear as spirits. Jesus answered that fear with things a spirit cannot do: be handled, show flesh and bones, and eat. Peter later preached that the apostles “ate and drank with Him after He arose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).

scene.label: “Peace to you”
scene.text: This was the everyday Hebrew greeting, shalom. On Jesus’ lips that night it fulfilled His promise in the upper room: “Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

scene.label: He breathed on them
scene.text: The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb when the Lord God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). As God once breathed life into Adam, Jesus breathes on His disciples as He gives the Spirit.

scene.label: Forgiving and retaining sins
scene.text: Christians read these words differently. Most Protestants understand them as authority to declare forgiveness through the gospel to all who believe and to warn those who refuse (Acts 10:43). Catholic and Orthodox Christians link them with absolution given by ordained ministers.

scene.label: The manuscripts
scene.text: Mark’s sentence about this evening (16:14) belongs to Mark 16:9–20. The NKJV prints the passage and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts do not include it.

witnesses.matthew: Does not record this event. Matthew tells of no appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem and moves from the women and the guards straight to the meeting on the mountain in Galilee (28:16–20).
witnesses.mark: Mark’s longer ending gives the evening one sentence and keeps only the rebuke. These verses stress the disciples’ unbelief three times (16:11, 13, 14), so the commission that follows goes to men who first had to be corrected.
witnesses.luke: Luke records the physical proofs: hands and feet, flesh and bones, and fish eaten in front of them. His account answers anyone who would call the risen Jesus a vision, and in Acts he says Jesus showed Himself alive “by many infallible proofs” (Acts 1:3).
witnesses.john: John records the peace, the sending and the breath of the Spirit, as Jesus’ mission passes to His followers. He also introduces Thomas’s demand for proof, which leads a week later to the high point of his Gospel.

seeing.reveals: The risen Jesus is the same Jesus, in a real body that bears His wounds and eats with His friends. He speaks peace to the men who abandoned Him and then shares His own mission with them: as the Father sent Him, He sends them.
seeing.living: Jesus came through shut doors to frightened people, and His first word was peace, not blame. But His peace came with a commission. Those He forgives He also sends, with His Spirit and a message of forgiveness for others.
seeing.ponder: What fear keeps your doors shut, and what would change if you heard the risen Jesus say to you, “Peace to you,” and then, “I also send you”?

preaching.big_idea: The wounded, risen Jesus gives peace to fearful disciples and sends them as the Father sent Him.
outline: The Spirit and the message of forgiveness (22–23)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus speaks peace twice (20:19, 21). The first time, He shows His wounds and their fear turns to gladness. The second time, He sends them out. The peace He gives is the peace they carry.
